content.thinking:
I can run the build in Node as a smoke test, including reading `b.root`, and validate the geometry there too—computing bounds, parts count, and triangle counts. Now I'm starting to write the file with imports for Three.js utilities and the builder setup.

Writing module imports...

I'm checking that `OutlinePoint` is exported properly from the builder module, then defining the `build()` function with the base joint setup and helper functions for creating simple geometry primitives like spheres, cylinders, and boxes.

Defining camel geometry logic...

Writing radius interpolation logic...

I'm checking that the body bottom connects correctly to the legs at the hip, and reconsidering leg proportions—right now they look stubby compared to a real camel's long legs relative to body depth, but I'm leaning toward keeping that cuter, more whimsical ratio.

Raising the center height to .44 gives legs visible at .28, with the hump and head stacking up proportionally. Scaling by .7 keeps things balanced against the tent height, so I'll set standing yC to .44 and figure out how kneeling drops that value down.

Working out the kneeling pose now: dropping by .23 puts the belly resting just above the folded legs. I'm mapping out the leg joint positions for both standing and kneeling stances -- shoulder to knee to hoof for the front legs, and hip to hock to hoof for the hind legs, adjusting the bend angles so the camel looks properly folded down when resting.

Now I'm adding the foot pad cylinder with a hoof color, and working out the kneeling leg pose where the front legs fold with the knee touching the ground and the lower leg tucked back under the chest.

Still shaping the limb and neck curves...

Still working out the neck and head geometry...

Defining head loft stations...

Defining the lower jaw loft segments with their widening widths and camel-colored tip, then placing a bulbous upper lip sphere at the muzzle for that whimsical open-mouth look.

Now I'm positioning the eyes with white spheres and dark pupils angled forward, adding small lash spikes pointing up-outward, and considering a hemisphere eyelid cap using a partial sphere geometry for a drooping lid effect.

I'm sketching brow ridges above each eye, cone-shaped ears with inner pink details, and a forelock of spikes at the top of the head, plus a scaled-up baby version with a bigger head and eyes. Then I'm working out a closed catmull-rom sweep for a red bridle ring around the muzzle, defining its elliptical path with specific radii.

Adding bridle details...

Now I'm planning the tail as a tapering sweep path with shrinking radius down to a tuft of dark downward-pointing spike cones at the end.

For the hump, I'm figuring out placement for small fur-like spikes along the top, computing the surface point by combining the body path position with the radius and bump offsets at that curve parameter.

Now I'm working out where to drape cloth over the hump region, sizing it slightly larger than the body radius so it sits just above the surface, and planning gold trim bands at the edges by converting world points into the camel's local coordinate space.

Still writing paint pattern logic...

Now I'm figuring out where to place hanging baskets along the camel's flanks, computing the body half-width at the midpoint to position them symmetrically on either side.

I'm thinking about small connecting details like thin rope rods linking basket rims to the cloth, a dark chest pad for the kneeling figure, and how to hang a gold bell near the neck—deciding the strap/ring orientation is tricky so I'm considering simpler placements like attaching it near the cloth side instead.

This feels like enough detail work; I'll move on to footprints and other final touches before starting the actual ~900 lines of code, being careful with the coordinate transformations as I go.

Still writing coordinate math...

Now I'm computing the apothem for the octagonal tent walls and setting up the lathe call with its radius, segments, and spin parameters. I'm working out the paint function logic that determines facet colors by mapping the wrapped angle to which of the eight segments a vertex falls into.

I work out the facet index by rounding the angle divided by 45 and taking mod 8, then use that parity to alternate colors — teal versus cream on the wall facets with gold trim and a dark hem band, and red versus cream on the roof facets with gold seam lines between them.

I'm positioning doors and valance details using local-to-world transforms, extruding small hanging triangle shapes for the valance trim, and designing a `put()` helper that composes position, rotation, and scale for placing geometry.

For the tent's valance, I'm calculating each triangle's world position and outward-facing rotation around the circle, then figuring out the angular spacing so each facet gets two triangles symmetrically offset from its center.

Now I'm working out the facet geometry for the roof decorations, placing 24 small triangles across the facets with alternating colors, then moving on to figuring out where the door arch sits relative to the front facet.

For the eave underside, I'm tracing how the wall top edge flares outward and upward to the lip, creating a gap where the roof hangs past the wall before meeting the door arch below it.

Now I'm planning additional details: a porch with poles and awning for tent 1, finial balls on the poles, and then moving to the campfire scene. I'm placing the campfire with a ring of rocks, flames, a tripod pot, and seating logs, plus a second palm tree and some market goods near the camels.

Checking tent2's rotated footprint and front edge position so I can place palm trees, camels, and goods nearby without overlapping — nudging palm1 and the camels to clear the tent's front corner.

Since I can't verify this visually, I'm planning a numeric approach instead: writing a node script to compute each part's world-space bounding box, group them by tag, and detect overlaps directly. I also want to build a simple ASCII top-down raster of the scene so I can see the layout spatially, and I'm even considering writing a tiny software rasterizer to produce an actual image I could inspect.

I'm weighing colour handling for the rasterizer — using material.color per mesh, and for painted parts, sampling the baked paint texture via UVs if the mesh exposes vertex colors or a DataTexture I can read directly in node. This feels worthwhile since it gives me genuine visual feedback without violating the harness's two-render limit, as it's just a personal scratch tool.

Now I'm sketching a function that generates outline points for a palm frond shape, stepping along its length and varying width to taper toward the tip, then double-checking the point sequence makes geometric sense as I trace through the indices.

Setting step size to .076 with width tapering from .11 to .05 for faceted triangular teeth, then extruding the shape to 0.012 thickness.

For the right half I'm mirroring the geometry by flipping the y-axis and swapping thickness directions. Now writing the frond function that marches along a direction vector computing position, pitch, and width per segment for the V-fold shape...

Verifying the perpendicularity: t is horizontal and orthogonal to h, and since d combines h with a vertical offset, t stays perpendicular to d, and u inherits that orthogonality too. That checks out, so I just need to confirm whether the extrude function actually requires y to be perpendicular to x.

For leaflet widths I'm sketching tapered profiles per segment so fronds look widest near the middle rather than uniform, with around five subdivisions per segment, and I'm checking that overlapping half-extrudes at segment joins blend cleanly. Rib thickness at .012 feels a bit chunky for the low-poly look, so I'm considering dropping it to .009, and I'm marking rib coloring based on proximity to the leaflet's center line.

Now I'm working out the bunting rope connecting palm1's trunk to tent2's front ridge pole, computing endpoint A from the trunk path at a height around y=0.9 and endpoint B from tent2's ridge tip, then sagging the connecting line like a catenary. I'm placing small triangular flags every 0.07 units along that curve with cycling colors, each oriented so its face turns to meet the rope's horizontal direction.

But checking the actual distance between palm1 and tent2, the gap is too short for a satisfying string of flags, so I'm reconsidering and testing palm2 to tent1's pole top instead -- that span works out to roughly 0.73 units, which feels better for six flags, so I'm switching the bunting to run between those two points instead.

Now I'm working out the second bunting line, from tent2's finial to palm1, at about 0.55 units for five flags, and double-checking the pole height clears the roofline. Then I move into pinning down the actual layout coordinates: pond center, water extents, grass bank boundaries, and palm1's base position relative to the pond's edge.

I'm checking that palm1 falls just outside the elliptical bank boundary, then placing its lean and crown. I add palm2 with its height and lean direction, a smaller palm3 off to the side, and start positioning tent1 relative to palm2's base to measure the distance between them.

Working through the math, I find the tent's corner falls outside the base ellipse at the current radius, so I need to enlarge the tent base dimensions to contain the eave and valance properly.

Checking tent2's rotated corner against the ellipse boundary, computing the world-space offset from its yaw angle to see if it still fits within the allowed radius.

Now I'm positioning Camel A at its location with its facing direction and body length, figuring out where its head and tail extend to.

I'm continuing to check placements: the baby camel, kneeling Camel B, the campfire, and starting to work out where goods should sit relative to tent1's door, verifying each stays within the elliptical boundary.

For the market goods near tent2's front, I'm computing the front corner position using the ridge direction and rotation, then nudging the crate placement to avoid overlapping the door curtain while staying close to the palm tree base.

I realize palm1 at (.55,-.35) actually falls inside tent2's rotated footprint when I transform it into local coordinates, so I need to relocate it. Testing (0.3,-0.4) instead, I check the local x and z values again and confirm this position now sits just outside the tent's bounding box.

Shifting to check (0.28,-0.42), the trunk clears tent2 with its radius, and I verify spacing against camel B's position and extents to make sure there's no overlap there either. I also lean the palm so its crown lands near the pond's edge within the water's x-range, and start checking goods placement relative to tent2.

I'm checking distances for camel A's body and goods placement, then moving to verify tent1's clearance against palm2 and flagging a possible overlap between tent1 and camel B given B's yaw and body extension.

Shifting B slightly to fix the clearance, then working through cactus, sign, and pond decorations like lilies, rocks, and reeds, checking each placement against nearby elements for spacing.

Now I'm trying to place dunes along the scene's rim without overlapping the tents or camels, testing a few corner positions and rejecting ones that collide with existing objects.

Settling on final dune placement left and right of the base, then moving to reeds clusters near the pond edges and a ring of rocks around the pond's perimeter.

I'm layering the slabs by height: grass topping the base, a sandy wet rim above it, and the water surface sitting just slightly higher than the rim for a subtle depth effect.

Now I'm placing scene elements by height—tents and palms sitting right on the grass patch around the pond—and considering adding a cute detail of small hoof prints trailing from the camel toward the water, using flattened cylinders colored in darker sand tones positioned in an alternating left-right pattern along the path.

For the sign, I'm sketching an SVG with a wooden board background and bold serif "OASIS" text in brown, mounted as a textured plane on the front face of a box, with a mirrored second plane so it reads correctly from both sides.

I'm planning the rigging for the hanging elements: the sign board hinges from a post's crossbeam via a pivot joint with a slight swing angle, and the lantern hangs similarly from an arm near one of the tents, each using bone-based joints for a natural hanging pose.

I'm also finalizing the color palette, picking hex values for sand, rock, and other surfaces while keeping the flat-color count under the limit, since paints and textures used for shading don't count toward that total. Now I'm ready to write the complete code in organized sections.

Still defining the color palette...

Now I'm planning a generic rod helper function to reduce repetition when creating cylindrical segments with configurable sides, then moving on to writing the actual file.

I should use `glow` for highlights, set loft station arrays with explicit width/height values, and use fewer sides with flat shading for the camel head sections. I'm also noting the sweep caps option and planning to flush the paint bucket before returning, then do a typecheck and smoke test once the ~700-line file is written.

input.command: mkdir -p scratch/desertOasisDiorama; sed -n 1,60p src/index.ts; grep -n "OutlinePoint" src/builder.ts | head
